commit.message:
8393085: AArch64: implement compact uncommon trap sequence

Prior to this change, uncommon trap sequences in C2 were implemented as
static Java calls - involving unnecessary spilling and post-call NOPs.

Introduce MachUncommonTrapNode. The node represents transition to the
uncommon trap blob. It is a safepoint, however - unlike static Java
calls - it does not require spilling of values from registers, because
all values are preserved by the uncommon trap blob at the entry point.
This substantially reduces size of C2-compiled methods.

The sequence consists of a BL followed by int32 trap_request literal.
The uncommon trap handler does not return to the call site, however
the BL is needed instead of B to provide information on location of
the trap sequence and its trap_request value.

The experimental option PreferCallBasedUncommonTraps is introduced
for debugging purposes and is intended to be removed soon.

The measurements have been run on Arm Neoverse N1, Neoverse V1 and
Neoverse V2 CPUs. Positive values represent improvement: reduction
in ms/op for performance, and reduction in KB for code cache sizes.
Code cache sizes are based on -XX:+PrintCodeCache max_used value.

Each workload has been run in 20 interleaved pairs of the baseline
and the patched versions. Order of the configurations in each pair
was chosen randomly. Each of these runs has been run as one JMH fork
with 30 warm-up iterations and 30 measurement iterations. Only the
final score reported by JMH has been considered a data point, while
all per-iteration measurement results were ignored.

In order to reduce impact on performance comparison from possible
profile differences, the same AOT-cached profile was used in each
run of the same workload. The AOT-cache was not, however, shared
across measurements for different CPUs. Each AOT-cached profile
was collected using a training run with 100 warm-up iterations and
100 measurement iterations.

The values in the tables are geometric means across all pairs for
the same workload. Positive values indicate improvements for both
performance and code cache size.

The * symbol marks performance measurements which, based on
additional analysis, appear to be statistically significant.
The ~ symbol marks workloads with performance behaviour that
appears to be multi-modal.
